stages.title: Advanced literary analysis
stages.hook: Two sentences say the same fact, yet one feels warm and the other cold. What differs?
explain: Close reading attends to how a text makes meaning through diction (word choice), syntax (sentence structure), tone, imagery, structure and sound. The question moves from what a passage says to how and why it says it that way.

Narrative technique matters. Free indirect discourse, used skilfully by Jane Austen, slides between narrator and character thought without quotation marks. Irony has types: verbal (saying the opposite of what is meant), situational (outcome contradicts expectation) and dramatic (audience knows more than characters). Intertextuality is the way texts echo and answer other texts.

Strong analysis builds an argument from patterns, tests it against counter-evidence, and attends to ambiguity, where a text supports more than one meaning. Context and form shape the reading, but evidence from the text is the anchor.

example.q: Analyse: "She was not unkind" versus "She was kind."
steps: The first uses litotes: a negative for understatement.
It suggests restraint or doubt about warmth.
The syntax changes tone from plain to guarded.

analogies.home: The same words said gently or sharply carry different meanings.
analogies.city: A headline's word choice frames a news event.
analogies.sport: A commentator's tone can make a draw sound like a disaster.
analogies.tech: Textual analysis tools count words, but close reading hears tone.

stages.mnemonic: How, not just what: diction, syntax, tone, structure.
terms: Narration that blends narrator and character thought.
Relations between texts through echo or allusion.
Capacity of language to support more than one meaning.

misc.wrong: The goal of analysis is to find the one hidden meaning.
misc.right: Good readings are evidenced arguments; ambiguity can be a feature rather than a puzzle with a single answer.

stages.limits: Some critics warn that close reading can neglect context and history.

trip.prompt: Look at how a short passage is analysed line by line.

teach.model: Close reading studies diction, syntax, tone, imagery and structure. It builds an evidenced argument and considers ambiguity. Irony may be verbal, situational or dramatic. Intertextuality links works.

stages.title: Shakespeare's major tragedies
stages.hook: Shakespeare's great tragedies were written within a few years of each other. What do they share, and where do they differ?
explain: Between about 1599 and 1608 Shakespeare wrote Julius Caesar, Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth, Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus. A. C. Bradley's Shakespearean Tragedy (1904) shaped the idea of the tragic hero with a fatal flaw, though later critics stress society, politics and language.

Hamlet survives in different early texts, so editors choose among versions. Its famous question, "To be, or not to be, that is the question", frames doubt about action and existence. Macbeth (c. 1606) was written under King James I; its equivocation, as when "Fair is foul, and foul is fair", plays on deceptive language. Othello explores jealousy, racism and manipulation; Coleridge called Iago's evil "motiveless malignity", though critics offer many motives. King Lear is bleak: the line "Nothing will come of nothing" begins a plot about words, love and nature. For long, Nahum Tate's 1681 version with a happy ending replaced the original on stage.

Julius Caesar asks whether the killing of a leader to save a republic can be justified, and Mark Antony's "Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears" shows rhetoric turning a crowd. Interpretation changes across time, with feminist, postcolonial and political readings of the same plays.

steps: He claims not to praise Caesar but does.

analogies.home: A family inheritance dispute is Lear's plot in miniature.
analogies.city: Modern political speeches use Antony's techniques.
analogies.sport: A manager's words can swing a crowd.
analogies.tech: Online rumour is Iago's method at scale.

terms: Language with double meaning, used to mislead.

misc.wrong: Shakespeare tragedies have one fixed text and one fixed meaning.
misc.right: Early texts differ and productions and criticism read the plays in many ways.

stages.limits: Debates continue about Hamlet's delay, Iago's motives and Lear's ending.

teach.model: Shakespeare's great tragedies include Hamlet, Macbeth, Othello, King Lear and Julius Caesar. They explore doubt, ambition, jealousy, pride and political violence. Early texts vary and critics read the plays in different ways.

stages.title: Shakespeare's comedies, histories and romances
stages.hook: How do plays that mix grief and laughter, or turn from jealousy to forgiveness, fit into categories like comedy and tragedy?
explain: Shakespeare's comedies play with love, gender and social order. In Twelfth Night, Viola's disguise raises questions about gender and desire. In As You Like It, Rosalind directs her own courtship in Arden. Some plays, called problem plays, such as Measure for Measure and All's Well That Ends Well, mix comedy with moral difficulty.

The history plays fall into two groups: the first tetralogy (Henry VI parts 1-3 and Richard III) and the second (Richard II, Henry IV parts 1 and 2 and Henry V). E. M. W. Tillyard argued they present a providential Tudor myth, while later critics such as those influenced by new historicism see doubt and subversion about power.

The late romances, Pericles, Cymbeline, The Winter's Tale and The Tempest, feature lost children, long separations, wonders and reconciliation. In The Winter's Tale, a king's jealousy destroys his family and the play ends with a statue that seems to come to life. The Tempest follows the exiled Prospero, his spirit Ariel and Caliban, and has been read in postcolonial terms as a drama of power over an island.

example.q: Place the play: a magician on an island controls a spirit and a native inhabitant.
steps: The island belongs to The Tempest.

analogies.home: Forgiveness after a long family quarrel is a romance ending.
analogies.city: Debates over who rules a territory echo The Tempest.
analogies.nature: The sea storm opens The Tempest.

stages.mnemonic: Comedy marries, history reigns, romance reunites.
terms: A play that mixes comic form with serious moral issues.
A group of four related plays.
A late play of loss, wonder and reconciliation.
Criticism relating literature to the culture and power of its time.

misc.right: The categories were used by the First Folio but many plays cross boundaries.

stages.limits: The Tempest's colonial readings are debated; some critics warn against reducing it to allegory.

stages.title: Literary criticism
stages.hook: Does the meaning of a poem live in the author's mind, in the words on the page, or in the reader? Critics have fought over this for a century.
explain: Literary criticism is the study and evaluation of literature. Different schools ask different questions. Formalism and the New Criticism (T. S. Eliot, I. A. Richards, Cleanth Brooks) treat the text as an autonomous object to be read closely, arguing against relying on the author's intention. Marxist criticism examines class and economic power. Psychoanalytic criticism applies ideas from Freud and others. Feminist criticism studies gender and representation. Postcolonial criticism, associated with Edward Said's Orientalism (1978), examines colonial power and representation.

Reader-response theory (for example Wolfgang Iser and Stanley Fish) argues that meaning is produced in the act of reading. Structuralism looks for underlying systems of signs. Deconstruction, associated with Jacques Derrida, argues that texts contain tensions that undermine stable meaning.
No school gives the complete answer. A strong critic knows the assumptions behind a method and uses evidence from the text, noting what each approach reveals and what it leaves out.

example.q: Match question to school: "How does this novel show class conflict?"
steps: The question focuses on class and economic power.
It uses the text as evidence for social structure.

analogies.home: Family members read the same letter differently depending on their experience.
analogies.city: Critics, like judges, argue from different principles.
analogies.tech: Different search methods find different results in the same data.
analogies.music: The same score gets very different performances.

Criticism that stresses the reader's role in meaning.
Criticism that examines colonial legacies in texts.

misc.right: In literary studies criticism means careful analysis and interpretation.

stages.limits: Schools overlap and critics often combine approaches.

teach.model: Literary criticism studies and interprets literature. New Criticism stresses close reading. Marxist, feminist, psychoanalytic and postcolonial approaches ask about class, gender, mind and empire. Reader-response stresses the reader. Each method reveals and hides.

stages.title: Comparative world literature
stages.hook: If tragedy appears in Athens, Lagos and Tokyo, is it one universal form, or just a Western word for many different things?
explain: Comparative literature studies works across languages, cultures and periods. It looks for shared forms and themes but also for differences, avoiding the assumption that one tradition is the measure of others.

Epic is an example. The Epic of Gilgamesh from Mesopotamia is among the oldest surviving literary works. The Iliad, Mahabharata, Shahnameh and Sundiata each tell of heroes and communities, but with distinct values and performance contexts. Tragedy offers another case: Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart gives Okonkwo features of a tragic hero but is also a story of a community changing under colonial rule. Japanese Noh drama, by contrast, shapes sorrow through ritual, masks and ghosts rather than plots of downfall.

Translation and world literature raise questions about who reads what and how texts circulate. Goethe popularised the idea of Weltliteratur in the 1820s. David Damrosch describes world literature as writing that gains meaning by circulating beyond its home culture. Comparison should respect context and avoid forcing one culture's categories on another.

steps: Both fall through a mix of choice and forces beyond them.
Differences: Okonkwo's fall is tied to colonial change and community values.

analogies.home: Families tell similar lessons in different tales.
analogies.city: Multilingual cities show many literary traditions side by side.
analogies.sea: Trade routes carried stories between lands.

stages.mnemonic: Compare to illuminate, not to rank.

misc.wrong: Comparing literatures means finding that they are all the same.

stages.title: Modern and postcolonial literature
stages.hook: When a writer uses the language of a former colonial power, is that a trap or a tool?
explain: Modernist writers in the early 20th century broke with older forms. T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922) and James Joyce's Ulysses (1922) used fragmentation and allusion, and Virginia Woolf used stream of consciousness to follow the flow of thought.

Postcolonial literature responds to colonial rule and its aftermath. Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart answered European accounts of Africa, taking its title from W. B. Yeats's "Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold". Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o argued in Decolonising the Mind (1986) that African writers should write in African languages, and he began writing in Gikuyu. Achebe defended writing in English transformed by African usage. Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) retells Jane Eyre from the perspective of the colonial Caribbean, and Derek Walcott's Omeros (1990) reworks the epic in the Caribbean. Salman Rushdie's Midnight's Children (1981) joins magical realism with Indian history.
Many contemporary writers, such as Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, write about migration, identity and memory across borders. Debates continue about language, audience, publishing and who controls stories.

example.q: Connect: Wide Sargasso Sea and Jane Eyre.
steps: Rhys takes a silent character from a Victorian novel.

analogies.home: Languages in a family reflect migration histories.

stages.mnemonic: Write back, rethink language, remember history.

stages.title: Advanced poetry analysis
stages.hook: How do poets get so much out of line breaks, sounds and silence?
explain: Advanced poetry analysis attends to form, sound and sense together. Scansion marks the stressed and unstressed syllables; poets vary a regular metre, such as iambic pentameter, for effect. Enjambment runs a sentence over a line break; a caesura is a pause within a line; end-stopped lines pause at the line end.

Sound devices include assonance (repeated vowel sounds), consonance (repeated consonants) and alliteration. Dickinson often used slant rhyme, where sounds nearly rhyme. Gerard Manley Hopkins used sprung rhythm. John Donne's metaphysical conceits link far-apart ideas, such as lovers and the legs of a compass.

Voice and persona matter: the speaker of a poem is not always the poet. In Shakespeare's Sonnet 73, "That time of year thou mayst in me behold", images of autumn, twilight and dying fire build a mood of ageing, and the couplet turns toward love. In Dickinson's "Because I could not stop for Death", death is courteous and the pace is calm, which changes how we feel about dying.

example.q: Analyse the line: "Because I could not stop for Death — / He kindly stopped for me —"
steps: Death is personified as a gentle driver.
Calm tone contrasts with a grave subject.
example.a: Personification and tone create calm irony.

analogies.home: A lullaby's rhythm soothes by pattern.

misc.right: The speaker is a persona; poets may invent voices very unlike themselves.

stages.limits: Scansion systems differ and some lines can be scanned more than one way.

teach.model: Poetry analysis looks at metre, line breaks and sound. Enjambment carries a sentence over a line. A caesura is a pause. Assonance and consonance are sound patterns. The speaker may be a persona. Conceits link far ideas.

stages.title: Dramatic writing and interpretation
stages.hook: A director cuts half the lines of a play and sets it in a different era. Is it still the same play?
explain: Dramatic writing builds on want, obstacle and stakes: a character wants something, faces opposition, and something important is at risk. Subtext lets characters hide what they feel. Pacing, entrances and exits and reversals keep a play moving.

Playwrights have reshaped the form. Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House (1879) brought realism and social questions to the stage. Anton Chekhov's The Cherry Orchard (1904) shows change through ordinary conversation. Bertolt Brecht's epic theatre aimed to make audiences think rather than lose themselves in emotion, using a technique called the alienation effect. Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot (1953) belongs to the Theatre of the Absurd, in which language and purpose seem to break down. Wole Soyinka's Death and the King's Horseman (1975) draws on Yoruba tradition and colonial conflict.

Interpretation is the performer's and director's part. The same script can be staged as satire, tragedy or farce. Choices about casting, setting, pacing and cuts change meaning. Shakespeare's plays have been set in many cultures and times; faithful interpretation attends to the text while allowing new emphasis.

example.q: Write the core of a scene: Amina needs money for school; her uncle refuses. Identify want, obstacle, stakes.
example.a: A scene driven by want, obstacle and stakes.

analogies.home: A family dinner can hold hidden conflict under polite talk.
analogies.sport: A match has want (win), obstacle (opponent) and stakes (title).
analogies.music: Performers interpret the same score differently.

stages.mnemonic: Want, obstacle, stakes; text plus choices equals production.
terms: Brecht's technique to keep audiences thinking critically.

misc.wrong: The script contains every choice a production will make.
misc.right: A script leaves space for directors and actors to decide emphasis, tone and meaning.

stages.limits: Debates continue about fidelity versus reinvention in staging classics.

stages.title: Cultural contexts and oral traditions
stages.hook: Can a story that was never written down be as precise as one in a book?
explain: Oral literature, sometimes called orature, is the art of spoken word: epics, praise poems, proverbs, riddles, tales and songs. Milman Parry and Albert Lord studied oral poets in the Balkans and proposed that formulas, repeated phrases and themes help poets compose epics aloud, an idea applied to Homer.

In West Africa, griots preserve genealogies, history and epics such as Sundiata with music, often on the kora. Praise poetry, such as Zulu izibongo, celebrates leaders and heroes. Ruth Finnegan's Oral Literature in Africa (1970) argued that oral art deserved study as literature. Māori carry genealogies (whakapapa) and histories in chant and speech, and Aboriginal Australian songlines map journeys across country in song.

Performance context matters: audience, music, gesture and occasion shape the work, and each performance is a new event. Cultural protocols matter too: some stories belong to families, clans or nations and may be restricted. Researchers work with communities and respect rules about who may share what. Writing down a tale does not freeze it, but it changes how it is experienced.

stages.limits: The Parry-Lord theory has been refined and criticised; not all oral traditions work the same way.
